newsitem.title: USA: US June industry output moderate, no pressure seen.
newsitem.headline: US June industry output moderate, no pressure seen.

text.p: U.S. industrial production in June offered an unsurprising view of moderate economic growth with no pressures building on resource use, economists said.

The Federal Reserve reported that U.S. industrial output rose 0.3 percent in June after rising a revised 0.2 percent in May. Economists polled by Reuters had given a consensus forecast for a 0.2 percent June output gain.
But the Federal Reserve revised May output down to 0.2 percent from the 0.4 percent originally reported.

Also, capacity utilization, the portion of the nation's factories, mines and utilities employed in that production, was 83.5 percent, unchanged from May. In a revision, May's capacity use figure was trimmed to 83.5 percent, from 83.7 percent originally reported.

The bond market responded positively to the report, or perhaps more accurately, to the combination of the two economic reports it got on Wednesday -- the June Consumer Price Index (CPI) and, less than an hour later, the Fed's industrial production report.

Anticipating a market-friendly CPI report, the market firmed in dealings before the CPI release at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up nearly a quarter of a point just before the CPI came out and gradually edged higher after it.
The bond rose to session highs after the industrial production report presented a picture of moderate economic growth with no pressures building on capacity.
At 0942 EDT/1342 GMT, the 30-year Treasury bond was up 16/32 to 101-17/32, yielding 6.51 percent.
The 30-year bond briefly reached a yield of 6.51 percent on Friday after the June Producer Price Index (PPI) report showed wholesale prices remained subdued.

"The industrial production report is about as expected," said Ram Bhagavatula, chief financial economist, Citicorp Global Finance N.A. "They revised May down a touch (to 0.2 percent from 0.4 percent) which is appropriate because we thought the May number looked high relative to other numbers we were seeing."
The capacity utilization portrait was also positive for the market, Bhagavatula said.
"We don't see any capacity pressures building," he said. "Capacity utilization is about where it's been for a whole year now."
Timothy Martin, senior economist at Nationsbank Corp, said the data helped to verify that the Fed would keep interest rates unchanged at its August 19 policy meeting.
"There is nothing new in the data to get them worried," said Martin.
"The data show moderate growth; respectable, moderate growth," said Charles Lieberman, chief economist at Chase Securities Inc.

"To the extent that the present growth rate is not putting a whole lot of pressure on capacity use, that means the inflation outlook remains reasonably benign which means that financial asset prices should do all right," said Bhagavatula.
